items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_brace.ex:160 — the "result must parse" guard only refuses an ambiguous `}` placement when the alternative placement would make the appended candidate unparseable; when the line after the unclosed literal begins with a binary operator both placements parse and mean different things, and the rule silently commits one. On `x = {1, 2` followed by a line `|> IO.inspect()` before `end`, the rule emits `x = {1, 2\n|> IO.inspect()}` — the tuple `{1, IO.inspect(2)}` — where the author plausibly meant `x = {1, 2}` piped into `IO.inspect`, i.e. `IO.inspect({1, 2})`. The output parses and compiles, so neither ProgressGuard nor the all-or-nothing commit can catch a wrong choice, and no test in the battery covers an operator-continuation line (the "ambiguous placement" tests only cover the case where the wrong placement fails to parse). The moduledoc (lines 35–44) says the rule "stays silent rather than picking a placement" for either-line ambiguities, which overstates the guard. The tokenizer-faithful placement is a defensible documented policy, but a human should decide whether to also refuse (or at least pin with a test) when the following line starts with an operator, since that is exactly the shape where the LLM's dropped `}` belongs one line up.

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_brace.ex:186 — the uniqueness guard only ever asks "would putting *all* the missing braces at the end of one earlier line also parse?" (`close_at(lines, earlier)` appends `String.duplicate("}", count)` to a single line). It never considers a placement *split* across two lines, so when the repair needs more than one `}` a second, differently-meaning reading can survive the guard unnoticed. Concrete input — `defmodule Example do` / `  def foo do` / `    x = {1, {2` / `    , 3` / `  end` / `end`: the target line `    , 3` takes two braces and yields `{1, {2, 3}}`, which parses, and the only earlier line (`    x = {1, {2`) parses with neither one brace (outer still open) nor two (`, 3` then becomes a standalone statement), so `sole_placement/3` returns `:ok` and the fix commits. The competing reading `{1, {2}, 3}` — inner closed on the first line, outer on the second — is equally faithful to the truncated source and is never tested. Output parses and compiles, so neither ProgressGuard nor the all-or-nothing commit can catch the wrong choice. Leading-comma continuation lines are rare in Elixir, so this is a narrow shape, but it is the same silent-behaviour-change class the guard was added for and the moduledoc's "placement must be beyond doubt" bullet (lines 46-58) reads as stronger than what the code checks. A human should decide whether to widen the guard to split placements, or narrow the moduledoc claim to "single-line placements".

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_brace.ex:192 — the "placement must be beyond doubt" guard only scans lines from `open_line - 1` downward, where `open_line` is whatever `Code.string_to_quoted/2` put in the error's `:line` field. When a literal leaves more than one `{` unclosed and those `{` sit on *different* lines (e.g. `x = {1,` on one line and `%{a: 2` on the next), that field names only one of them — on my reading of the tokenizer it is the innermost, because the error is raised against the top of the delimiter stack. If so, every line between the outer `{` and the inner one is never tried as a competing `}` placement, so on multi-line nested literals the uniqueness guard is weaker than the moduledoc's second bullet (lines 46-60) claims, and the same lines are also invisible to `split_placement?/3` (line 206), which shares the range. Nothing in either test file pins which `{` the parser names: every nested fixture (`..._analyze_test.exs:39`, `:51`; `..._fix_test.exs:145`) opens all of its braces on one line. The consequence is bounded — a `}` on a line before the inner `{` cannot close that inner `{`, and the leftover continuation lines are usually comma-led and would not stand alone as statements — but it is a coverage hole in exactly the guard two fix rounds were spent widening. A second-order effect of the same question: the issue's `meta.line` (line 96) would point at the inner `%{` rather than at the literal the user actually has to close.

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_brace.ex:190 — `repair/1` is quadratic-ish in reparses and the expensive path is the one that commits. For each candidate earlier line, `sole_placement/3` pays up to 5 whole-source `Code.string_to_quoted` calls in `close_at/2` plus up to 4x5 more in `split_placement?/3` — 25 reparses of the entire file per line — and `Enum.any?/2` only short-circuits when the input is ambiguous, i.e. when the rule *refuses*. `Credence.Syntax` then calls `analyze/1` and `fix/1` separately, so the whole scan is paid twice. An LLM-emitted attribute map spanning a few hundred lines whose lines do not end in `,` (values on their own continuation lines) therefore costs several thousand full-file parses before the rule fires. Memoizing `close_at/2` per line, or capping the scanned span, would remove it.

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_doc_heredoc.ex:73 — the rule's whole admission test is "the first non-blank line after `@doc \"\"\"` starts with `def`", which is also true of a *correctly closed* doc heredoc whose first content line is a `def` example. items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_doc_heredoc.ex:134 — because the scan stops only at a `def…` line, every module attribute between the doc text and the definition is swallowed into the doc. On `defmodule S do` / `  @doc """` / `  Adds.` / blank / `  @spec add(integer, integer) :: integer` / `  def add(a, b), do: a + b` / `end` the closer lands under the `@spec`, so the emitted module's `@doc` string ends with the spec text and the `@spec` attribute itself is gone. The result parses and compiles without a warning, so neither the per-rule guard nor the round's all-or-nothing gate can see the deleted contract. `@doc` → `@spec`/`@impl` → `def` is the ordering LLMs emit most often, and it is exactly the shape this rule exists to repair. Note this is a behaviour change from the base version, which declined this input outright (`next_nonblank_is_def?` saw the prose line and returned `false`): the PR trades "repairs nothing" for "repairs it wrongly, and the wrong answer ships".

The boundary that does this is `@attribute_word` (lib/syntax/close_unclosed_doc_heredoc.ex:90), a bare `^@\w+\b`, introduced by this PR in e626a92. The same PR (4d9ebd1, lib/syntax/close_unclosed_doc_heredoc.ex:79 and the test at :176) established the opposite policy for the identical kind of ambiguity — a `defstruct` line at the doc's indent is "as plausibly doc prose as it is code", so the rule declines rather than guess. A bare `@word` line is exactly as ambiguous, but here the rule guesses "code" and corrupts. Unlike the `defstruct` case there *is* something to tell them apart with: the repair this boundary exists to buy (`@doc` → `@spec` → `def`, test at :420) only needs the doc-adjacent attributes, so restricting `@attribute_word` to a known set (`@doc`, `@spec`, `@impl`, `@deprecated`, `@since`, `@doc`-family) — or declining, as the `defstruct` branch does — would keep every repair this file asserts while dropping the corruption. A human should decide whether the cost is still worth pinning; the moduledoc documents it (lib/syntax/close_unclosed_doc_heredoc.ex:87-89), which is why this is a concern and not a blocker.

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_fn_delimiter.ex:167 — the repair is committed only if deleting the stray `end` makes the WHOLE file parse, so the rule silently declines on any file that carries a second syntax error anywhere — including a second instance of this very bug. Two `fn … end)` + stray-`end` mistakes in one file are repaired by neither this rule nor `NoUnclosedFnDelimiter` (whose `repair/1` likewise requires `parses?(fixed)`): the first rule's candidate deletions all still fail to parse because of bug #2, and the sibling's insert-only pass never parses either. items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_fn_delimiter.ex:154 — the comment credits the wrong mechanism. The downward scan only keeps the rule out of text *above* the insertion line; it does nothing about a bare `end` line inside a heredoc *below* it. What actually rules those out is the `parses?(candidate)` check: deleting a line inside a string/heredoc removes no `end` token, so the extra `end` is still unbalanced and the candidate never parses. Worth rewording, so that a future relaxation of the parse gate is not made on the belief that the scan direction is carrying the safety.

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_fn_delimiter.ex:259 — the identity guard `same_stray_end?/2` compares the `(` position captured *before* the deletion against the one reported *after* it, relying on the invariant stated at :159-161 and :236-240 that "the `(` is always above the line being deleted". Nothing checks that invariant. When `stray_end_error/1` picked up a `(` that is *below* the insertion point (the blocker above), deleting any bare `end` line shifts that `(` up by one line, the two positions differ, and the guard reads the unchanged error as "the stray `end` is gone" — so the very first bare `end` line at or below the insertion point is accepted no matter what it closes. The same positional-not-semantic weakness lets a deletion be accepted whenever the identical structural error is merely re-reported at a *different* enclosing `(`.

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_fn_delimiter.ex:262 — `stopped_at_or_below?/2` does not do what the comment at :241-245 says it does. That comment claims it rejects a deletion that removed a real enclosing `end`, because the resulting unterminated block "drags the error back above the repair". But this repo's own `Credence.Syntax.ProgressGuard` moduledoc (lib/syntax/progress_guard.ex:43-47) records the opposite: `meta[:end_line]` is **EOF** for an unclosed delimiter. A deletion that leaves a block unterminated therefore reports `end_line` at EOF, which always satisfies `line > deleted_idx`, so this guard passes exactly the case it is documented to catch. It is the only backstop left after the whole-file parse gate was removed, and it is doing far less than the comment asserts. (Related: the rule hand-rolls a progress measure that `ProgressGuard` already provides for this round.)

items.finding: lib/syntax/close_unclosed_fn_delimiter.ex:305 — "first `end` token below the repair is the stray one" is an assumption, not a property of the bug, and when it is false the rule deletes a real block terminator and the result parses, so nothing catches it. Input: the documented bug shape where the outer `fn` body continues with a complete `do…end` block before the dangling `end` — `defmodule M do / def go(m) do / Enum.map(m, fn r -> / Enum.map(r, fn e -> / if e == 0 do 1 else e end) / if r > 0 do / IO.puts("big") / end / r * 2 / end / end) / end / end`. After inserting `end` on line 5 the leftover complaint is `(` (line 3) closed by `end` (line 11), 3 <= 5, so `stray_end_above?` passes; `first_end_token_line/2` then stops at line 8 — the `if`'s own terminator — not at the real stray on line 10. Deleting line 8 yields `if r > 0 do IO.puts("big"); r * 2 end`, which parses and compiles cleanly, so `clears_stray_end?/3`'s `{:ok, _ast} -> true` arm accepts it unconditionally. The function now returns `nil` for `r <= 0` instead of always returning `r * 2` — a silent behaviour change, and `analyze/1` reports line 5 with "a stray `end` follows", which is a false diagnosis of that line. Pre-existing: the base version's "first bare `end` line whose removal makes the whole file parse" scan picks the same line 8 and commits the same output. What the PR changes is that the moduledoc (lines 79-83) and the `clears_stray_end?` comment (lines 339-346) now assert this deletion is ruled out "by the shape of the bug", so the hazard is now documented as handled. Note the guard is one-sided: it bounds walking *past* the stray but not stopping *short* of it.
